question.problem:
Given that $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,17),$ construct a statement that also must be true:

$$
a-{{field-1}}≡b-{{field-2}}\,(\text{mod}\,17)
$$
question.worked_solution:
The subtraction property states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Therefore, we can subtract the same integer from both sides of a congruence, keeping the modulus unchanged:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-5≡b-5\,(\text{mod}\,17)
$$

$$

$$
a-{{field-1}}≡b-{{field-2}}\,(\text{mod}\,9)
$$
question.worked_solution:
The subtraction property states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Therefore, we can subtract the same integer from both sides of a congruence, keeping the modulus unchanged:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-2≡b-2\,(\text{mod}\,9)

$$
a-{{field-1}}≡b\,(\text{mod}\,13)

question.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

This gives rise to the following facts:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,⟺\,a≡b+kn\,(\text{mod}\,n) \\ a≡b\,⟺\,a+kn≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can add a multiple of the modulus $13$ to one side of the congruence. Notice that 

$$
-26=(-2)\cdot 13.
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-26≡b\,(\text{mod}\,13)

question.problem:
A parodic holiday, International Talk Like a Pirate Day, was celebrated for the first time on September 19th, 1995. Given that January 1st, 1995, was a Sunday, use congruences to determine on which day of the week this holiday was celebrated for the first time.

*Hint: The year 1995 was not a leap year since it is not divisible by $4.$*
question.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1995, and September 1st, 1995. 

- There were $5$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July,  and  August).

- There were $2$ months with $30$ days (April and  June).

- There was $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and September 19th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to September 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(5)+30(2)+28(1)}}+18.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,28≡0,\,18≡4\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =5(31)+2(30)+1(28)+18 \\  & ≡5(3)+2(2)+1(0)+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡15+4+0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1+4+0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $2$ days after January 1st, 1995, namely Tuesday.

Jacopo Peri's Euridice, modern opera's earliest known, fully surviving work, was first performed in Florence on October 6th, 1600. Given that January 1st, 1600, was a Saturday, use congruences to determine the day of the week on which the opera was first performed.

*Hint: The year 1600 was a leap year since it's an end-of-century year (multiple of $100$) and divisible by $400.$*
question.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1600, and October 1st, 1600. 

- There were $5$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July, and August).

- There were $3$ months with $30$ days (April, June, and September).

- There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and October 6th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to October 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(5)+30(3)+29(1)}}+5.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,29≡1,\,5≡5,\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =5(31)+3(30)+1(29)+5 \\  & ≡5(3)+3(2)+(1)+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡15+6+1+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1+6+1+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡13\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡6\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date 6 days after January 1st, 1600, namely Friday.

question.problem:
Christmas in 2100 will be celebrated, as usual, on December 25th. Given that January 1st, 2100, is a Friday, use congruences to determine the day of the week on which Christmas will be celebrated in 2100.

*Hint: The year 2100 is not a leap year since it's an end-of-century year (multiple of $100$) and is not divisible by $400.$*
question.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 2100, and December 1st, 2100. 

- There are $6$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July, August, and October).

- There are $4$ months with $30$ days (April, June, September, and November).

- There is $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and December 25th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to December 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(6)+30(4)+28(1)}}+24.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,28≡0,\,24≡3\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =6(31)+4(30)+1(28)+24 \\  & ≡6(3)+4(2)+(0)+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡18+8+0+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4+1+0+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $1$ day after January 1st, 2100, namely Saturday.

*Hint: The year 2000 was a leap year since it's an end-of-century year (multiple of $100$) and divisible by $400.$*

- There were $3$ months with $30$ days (April, June, and September).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and November 4th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to November 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(6)+30(3)+29(1)}}+3.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,29≡1,\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =6(31)+3(30)+1(29)+3 \\  & ≡6(3)+3(2)+(1)+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡18+6+1+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4+6+1+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡14\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡0\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as January 1st, 2000, namely Saturday.
